title: Eight-pointed snowflake papercut
subtitle: Folding and cutting a symmetrical eight-pointed snowflake from a single square of paper
excerpt: An eight-pointed snowflake papercut uses a single square of paper folded to one-eighth of its area, then cut with a craft knife. When unfolded, the cuts produce eight-way symmetry. The technique is the same whether the paper is 10 cm or 60 cm square: only the scale changes. The finished snowflake can hang in a window, be pressed flat and framed, or be used as a decorative layer in papercutting compositions.
sourceNotes: Symmetrical snowflake papercutting is a traditional winter craft in European and North American traditions; no single source text is canonical. Method described here is an original Homemade pattern based on established folding geometry.

glossaryTerms.definition: A paper folding sequence that reduces a square to one-eighth of its area (a right-angled triangle with a folded edge on two sides and the open point on the third). Cuts made to this folded parcel appear in eight identical positions when the paper is unfolded.

content.text: : a square folded in half twice (giving four-way symmetry) and then folded diagonally once (giving eight-way symmetry). Every cut made to the resulting triangular parcel appears in eight identical positions in the unfolded snowflake. The design space is small and the cuts must be confident: tentative half-cuts leave ridges rather than clean holes.

items.name: Cartridge paper, 130 gsm, cut to a square
items.notes: For a first attempt, use a 20 cm square. Thinner paper (80 gsm) is harder to cut cleanly after folding; thicker paper (220 gsm) is too stiff to unfold without tearing. 130 gsm is the best weight for this technique.

items.name: Craft knife with fresh blade
items.notes: A fresh blade is essential. Dragging a dull blade through 8 layers of paper tears the snowflake arms. Change the blade before starting.

items.name: Bone folder
items.notes: For making sharp, clean folds. Each fold should be creased firmly before the next fold is made.

content.text: Start with a square of paper. Fold in half horizontally, crease firmly with the bone folder. Fold in half again vertically, crease firmly. The paper is now a quarter-size square. Fold diagonally from the double-folded corner to the open corner. Crease firmly. The resulting shape is a right-angled triangle, with the fully folded (double-closed) corner at the right angle. This is the base for all your cuts.

On the folded triangle, lightly pencil in your cut shapes. Three rules: never cut all the way across any arm of the triangle from one folded edge to the other (the snowflake will fall into pieces when unfolded); always leave at least 3 mm of paper at the tip of the triangle and along the folded edges; and place larger cuts near the centre and smaller, more detailed cuts near the outer edges. A simple first design: cut 3 triangular notches along each of the two non-folded edges of the triangle, and one curved notch near the tip.

Cut each pencilled shape cleanly with the craft knife. Cut each line in a single decisive pass rather than multiple sawing motions. After cutting, unfold slowly and gently: unfold the diagonal fold first, then the two square folds. Unfold on the cutting mat rather than lifting into the air, to avoid tearing the delicate cut arms before the paper is fully flat.

items.cause: Cuts extended too close to or across a folded edge, leaving too little paper to hold the arms together.
items.fix: Leave at least 3 mm of paper at every folded edge and tip. On a 20 cm square (folded to a 7 cm triangle), 3 mm is easy to maintain. On a smaller square, increase the margin to 4 to 5 mm proportionally.

items.symptom: The cut edges are ragged rather than clean
items.cause: The blade is too dull to cut cleanly through 8 layers of cartridge paper.
items.fix: Replace the blade before starting. On a 20 cm square folded to 8 layers of 130 gsm paper, a blade that felt sharp for one cut may be dull enough to drag on the next.
